title: Artificial intelligence
theory: Treat generated output as a proposal

An answer can sound confident and still be incorrect. Define what correctness would mean, inspect the proposed implementation, and test it against that contract. Do not confuse fluent explanation with verified behavior.
Write a fixed set of cases and expected outcomes before comparing approaches. Keep some cases separate from those used to revise the implementation. Record failures, not only successes.

Record where a suggestion came from, what you changed, and what evidence supports it. Do not upload confidential or operational data. These exercises need no paid model API and can use the deliberately flawed samples provided.

This is an unofficial companion with original exercises. For official Harvard submissions, follow Harvard's current academic-honesty policy. Assistance is recorded in this course rather than being silently counted as independent work.

quiz.prompt: A generated program passes its one demonstration. What follows?
options: Test it against additional specified cases
quiz.explanation: A single demonstration is weak evidence for the full contract.

quiz.prompt: What best distinguishes a claim from evidence?
options: A reproducible observation or source supporting the claim
quiz.explanation: Evidence can be inspected or reproduced.

quiz.prompt: You use the same cases to repeatedly tune a solution and to report final performance. Risk?
quiz.explanation: A separate evaluation set helps reveal failure to generalize.

quiz.prompt: What should you submit to an external model for this course?
quiz.explanation: Use synthetic examples and protect private or restricted material.

quiz.prompt: Two implementations both work. What else is useful to compare?
quiz.explanation: Correctness is necessary but design trade-offs still matter.

quiz.prompt: An AI-assisted completion should be recorded as?
quiz.explanation: Assistance and the evidence supporting the result should remain visible.

tasks.title: Audit a confident but wrong claim
tasks.brief: A generated note claims: "binary search works on any array because it checks the middle."
requirements: Construct an unsorted array and target that refute the claim for ordinary binary search.
Trace the algorithm and identify the invalid assumption.
Rewrite the claim with the needed precondition.
Attach a reproducible test or trace; no external model is needed.

tasks.brief: Turn the repaired average into a small reproducible evaluation exercise.
requirements: Define at least six cases spanning ordinary, negative, fractional, singleton, and empty inputs.
Use part of the cases for development and keep the others untouched until evaluation.
Report the exact passed/total counts without claiming broad statistical accuracy.
Record assistance used and any failures discovered.

Repair the transformation and test a fresh case.
Explain the difference between sorting and deduplication without copying the earlier average audit.

tasks.title: Project AI: evidence-first code review
tasks.brief: Add a code-review record to your project.
requirements: Review one generated or deliberately flawed suggestion against written requirements.
Record source/provenance, tests, results, and the final decision.
Keep the evaluation reproducible without an external paid service.
Document which parts were authored, assisted, and independently checked.
